before: count := 3 declares a variable whose inferred type is int. Type inference does not make its type change on each assignment.
int is either 32 or 64 bits depending on the implementation. int64 explicitly selects a signed 64-bit type; float64 represents approximate fractional values.
A constant such as 3 can be used where a compatible numeric type is expected if its value fits. A typed numeric variable follows stricter assignment rules.
Two integer operands produce an integer result. A floating-point operand can make this division floating-point.
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare integer and floating operands, then inspect why the result type differs without assuming int is always 32 bits. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A type tells Go what kind of value something holds. With `:=`, Go works out the type from the starting value. That variable keeps its type later.
`int` holds whole numbers. Its size can differ between computers. `int64` has a fixed size. `float64` can hold fractions, but some values are approximate.
A constant is a value that does not change. A number written without a fixed type can fit different number types, as long as its value is allowed.
When both numbers in this division are integers, Go keeps only the whole-number answer. It drops the fraction rather than rounding up.
The screen shows `2`. The integer calculation 5 / 2 drops the fractional part.
Change 5 to `5.0` in the same example. That makes this a floating-point calculation, which can keep a fractional answer. Go then chooses float64 for result.
